extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; lawmakers and reformers considering constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conditions for when representative government is admissible, durable, and beneficial for a people; identifies social, moral, and institutional requisites and countervailing circumstances where other forms (despotism, monarchy, central authority) may be preferable. Useful for assessing constitutional reform and civic-readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental condition 1 — willingness to receive it
rubrics_metrics.description: That the people should be willing to receive it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill lists this as the first of three fundamental conditions. If public opinion is indifferent or hostile, representative institutions are unlikely to take permanent root; indifference and inability to understand processes are often as fatal as active opposition. Example: the executive will overpower unbacked representative bodies; permanence requires readiness of the people to fight for institutions when endangered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental condition 2 — willingness and ability to preserve it
rubrics_metrics.description: That they should be willing and able to do what is necessary for its preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative institutions depend for permanence on effective public opinion and feeling that can check the executive; lacking this, the executive can set aside or subdue representative organs. Guidance includes assessing whether citizens will support institutions against coups or executive encroachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental condition 3 — willingness and ability to discharge duties
rubrics_metrics.description: That they should be willing and able to fulfill the duties and discharge the functions which it imposes on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens must take on the obligations of participation (electorate responsibility, public duties); absent interest, suffrage is used for private/local ends, assemblies become place-hunting bodies. Examples: benefit of public functions (jury, parish offices) in educating citizens; negative: if nobody is engaged, representatives pursue private fortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active,self-helping character of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: A people with an active, self-helping character (energy, striving, habit of exertion) is best adapted to representative government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues activity and self-reliance cultivate public spirit and lessen envy; such peoples (e.g., England, the United States) are likelier to create and sustain institutions that improve inward nature as well as outward conditions. Anti-pattern: energy directed to trivial ends still preferable to inactivity, because it builds capacities and mechanical progress that later enable intellectual/social advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive/submissive character (habit of obedience) is a hindrance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where people need to learn obedience or are extremely submissive, representative government may be unsuitable and even impedimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribes trained in energy but not obedience will reflect turbulence in assemblies; such peoples often require a despotic or military authority to instill the habit of obedience. Example: some early societies learn submission via military command or a single superior; prophets or military chiefs can exercise temporary authority but seldom create lasting civic habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to form public opinion and sustained civic interest
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be sufficient public interest in general affairs to form effective public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only a small fraction cares for the general good, electors will vote for private/local interests and assemblies become corrupt or ineffectual. Even where representatives do little good, they may preserve ideas of popular rights and liberty of the press (example: modern Greece), but this depends on other stabilizing factors (e.g., an hereditary king). Assess whether the populace has the habit of caring about collective as opposed to merely private concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation in occasional public functions educates citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional demand on citizens to exercise public functions (jury service, parish offices, dicasteries) raises their intellectual and moral standard and fosters public spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill cites Athens' ecclesia/dicastery and English jury/parish office service as formative civic education. Guidance: evaluate whether existing institutions give citizens real opportunities to deliberate on collective interests and apply public-minded principles; lack of such experience yields narrow private morality and absence of identification with the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and complexity make representation necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Since not all can personally participate in public business in communities larger than a small town, representative government is the ideal form: the admission of all to sovereign power must be ultimate aim but mediated by representatives in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill holds that while universal personal participation is impossible in large polities, representative institutions should be as participatory as the community's improvement allows; the ideal is representative government when the whole people participate indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government incompatible with rulers who manage subjects' business for them
rubrics_metrics.description: Irresponsible rulers who supersede citizens' free agency favor the passive type of character and repress self-helping qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The habit of being managed precludes citizens' internal activity; even when rulers do not consciously repress, the position of autocracy itself restrains endeavour by certainty of impotence. Example: regulatory control of French manufactures by Colbert as an instance of managerial repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit of locality / lack of national cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: An inveterate spirit of locality and absence of feelings/sympathies to form a nation make representative government less appropriate; such political atoms may need central authority to coalesce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that regions with strong local identities rarely coalesce voluntarily into a nation; historical cases show central rule often welds disparate communities into a people. Preferred interim: a representative body auxiliary to a central power, educating local chiefs toward national feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the mass is degraded relative to a superior caste
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a small leading portion of the population is markedly superior in civilization to the remainder, immediate government by representatives of the whole may harm the superior class's ability to uplift the masses, and pure rule by the superior ranks may entrench degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill suggests the best prospect is an authority in the chief ruler of the dominant class, possibly with subordinate representative bodies of the superior caste that can be expanded over time. Examples: English Parliament history; possible role of a monarch of extraordinary genius (Charlemagne, Peter the Great) though such accidents are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative assemblies will mirror popular defects (prejudice, ignorance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudices, old habits, ignorance, and deficiencies of national character prevalent in a people will be faithfully reflected in their representative assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the executive administration is comparatively free from such defects, more good may be achieved by rulers not hampered by the need to carry ill-informed assemblies. Exception: when rulers are foreigners or of superior civilization, their rule can accelerate improvement (colonial example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive desire to exercise power over others (place-hunting) undermines liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the passion for governing others is stronger than desire for personal independence, representative institutions tend to become place-hunting mechanisms that favor overgovernment and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a people prefers open competition for offices rather than restraints on government; examples: tendencies in some Southern European contexts and Spanish America leading to chronic revolution or concentration of despotism; contrasted with English avoidance of place-hunting where advancement is sought in business/profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government may be inapplicable where it prevents acquisition of needed habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government can be an impediment if people must first acquire certain moral or civic habits (obedience, cohesion) which the presence of full representation would prevent them from learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill holds kingly or central authority may be the most suitable form in early stages of development to inculcate habits necessary for later representative institutions. Examples: serf emancipation under centralized monarchy (French history) or necessity in parts of Europe and Russia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of participation should match general improvement and aim at universal admission
rubrics_metrics.description: The participation should everywhere be as great as the general degree of improvement of the community will allow; ultimately nothing less than admission of all to a share in sovereign power is desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill treats incremental expansion of participation as a policy aim: any participation, even smallest public functions, is useful; evaluate existing institutions by whether they broaden and educate participation toward fuller representation.
